subject: convert long nested for loops to apply

messages.author: ecf19e9eac4d03c4
messages.subject: convert long nested for loops to apply
parts:
Hi All,

I have a task that's in essence simple to do, but that's taking way too long to finish in R.  It's the sort long loop task (in this case over 500,000 iterations) that one should not do in R, but since I was working in R already I tried doing it in R.  I initialized an empty object of the correct dimension and let it run for ~11 hours, but it still wasn't done  ...so I stopped it.

Although I'm about to shift to python to accomplish what I need, I'm now curious as to whether or not it can be done in R at reasonable speed with apply().  I couldn't figure out how to do it with apply(), so I defaulted to fro loops.

I have a genotypic matrix that has 440 genotype lines of a QTL population as its rows and 1049 "bins" as its columns.  The "bins" are genomic chunks at which the entire population is either homozygous for parent-1 = 0, heterozygous = 1, or homozygous for parent-2 = 2; essentially for a given bin a line has 0, 1, or 2 depending on its genotype at that bin.

What I'm trying to do is to take this genotypic matrix and expand its columns to include all pairwise epistatic interactions among the 1049 bins.  The epistatic columns' "genotype" is simply the multiplication of a given pair of bin genotype vectors.  I tried to do this with nested for() loops, as you can see in the attached R script.  However, it's just way too slow in R, which I kind of feared it would be.  After all, it's 549676 new columns that need to be calculated, inserted, and named.  As I said, I tried to speed it up by appending an empty matrix of the correct size to the original matrix (knowing that R takes longer if it has to resize/enlarge objects), but it's still taking way too long.

So, I'm hoping that y'all can help turn my nested loops into an apply() or nested apply()s.  I'm attaching my code and the genotype matrix.

By the way, I think the combn() function may be able to do what I need, but I don't know if I can feed it a matrix and am still getting my head around how to structure the custom function to use with combn() to achieve what I need.  I'm thinking that I can feed combn() a list of the bin/column vectors instead of a matrix.

Thanks in advance for your help!!
Dan Fulop.

messages.author: b35e99045f6c74c2
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: convert long nested for loops to apply
parts:
Hi Dan,

No need to use apply(); combn() takes simplify=FALSE to it returns a list. This allows you to use mclapply() from the parallel package. With four cores on my Macbook Pro, this takes:

> system.time(tmp <- mclapply(combn(ncol(geno.mat), 2, simplify=FALSE), function(i) geno.mat[, i[1]] * geno.mat[, i[2]], mc.cores=4))
   user  system elapsed
 44.684  13.527  73.109

Then cbind() these together with:

res <- do.call(cbind, tmp)

which takes a few seconds. I haven't really checked the results, but they look like everything worked out (please double check!):

# quick check
> combn(ncol(geno.mat), 2, simplify=FALSE)[[1]]
[1] 1 2
> all(res[, 1] == geno.mat[, 1] * geno.mat[, 2])
[1] TRUE

Overall, this is the fastest approach. apply() won't be any faster because it can't be parallelized and choose(ncol(geno.mat), 2) * ncol(geno.mat) is a lot of floating point ops (and the most expensive part is likely accessing the columns unnecessarily in apply()).

Are you sure you want to multiply these 0, 1, 2 encoded genotypes for interactions? Having no alternate alleles (a 0) will zero out everything...

HTH,
Vince

messages.author: ecf19e9eac4d03c4
messages.subject: Re: [D-RUG]: convert long nested for loops to apply
parts:
Hi Vince,

Thanks a ton!!

As to multiplying the encoded genotypes, I was wrestling with this myself until I talked to Jie Peng, a statistician who's collaborated with us on previous QTL projects.  Sure, it implies a certain genetic architecture (both loci contribute equally to the epistatic effect and both must be present in order to have an effect), but relaxing those assumptions would require fitting additional parameters for which we don't have data.  Also, the individual (non-epistatic) bins are still included, so they're possible independent effect (independent of an epistatic effect) is still accounted for.

It might be worth pointing out that the QTL population is not a RIL pop., but rather a mix of BC2 and BC3 lines back-crossed to parent-1; parent-1 is encoded as 0, and is included in the phenotypic data and mapping analysis.  Perhaps the back-crossed design makes the choice of epistatic encoding more palatable?

Could you elaborate what you have in mind as an alternative to multiplication?

Incidentally, the purpose of building the expanded genotypic matrix is to use it in a penalized/regularized regression to infer additive and epistatic QTL simultaneously without restricting the epistatic interactions to those QTL that possess additive effects.  We're using a method (sparsenet) that implements the MC+ penalty family, which is a combination of L1 (lasso) and L0 (best subset) penalties.

Cheers,
Dan.
